name: AI readiness and use cases
title: AI readiness and use-case prioritisation
thesis: Before anyone builds, someone must decide what is worth building. An FDE checks whether the customer is ready (data, people, process, platform, risk), collects candidate use cases, scores them the same way, and picks a first pilot that is valuable, feasible and safe, then writes a roadmap the sponsor signs.
note: Read left to right along the top, then right to left along the bottom. The dashed box is the branch for ideas that fail the readiness check: they go to a list of gaps to fix, and come back later.
ideas: Readiness has five parts: data (does it exist and can you reach it), people (an owner and users with time), process (a stable workflow to change), platform (where it will run) and risk (legal, privacy, reputational).
A use-case discovery workshop turns vague interest ('we should use AI') into a list of specific tasks with a named user, a volume and a pain.
Score every idea on the same scale (for example 1 to 5 for value, feasibility, data availability and risk) so the choice is defensible and not a matter of who spoke loudest.
A good first pilot sits in the high-value, low-effort corner of the 2x2 and has clean enough data, a willing team and a measurable baseline.
For each idea decide build, buy or configure: many ideas are best served by a feature in a tool the customer already owns.
traps: Starting with the most exciting idea instead of the one with data, an owner and a baseline, so the pilot stalls on access in week three.
Scoring only value and ignoring data availability and risk, which is how teams end up piloting something legal will never approve.
Writing a roadmap with ten parallel pilots; a first customer usually has capacity for one or two.
qa: A customer's CEO says 'we want to do AI' but has no specific idea. What do you do in the first two weeks?

I run a short readiness check and a use-case workshop with the people who do the work. I collect 10 to 20 concrete ideas, each with a user, a volume and a pain, score them on value, feasibility, data availability and risk, and bring the top two or three to the sponsor with a recommendation for one pilot and what we need from them to start.
Two use cases score almost the same. How do you choose?

I look at the tie-breakers that decide whether a pilot finishes: whose data is already accessible, which team has an owner with time, which has a clean baseline to measure against, and which carries less risk. I also prefer the one that teaches us something reusable for the second use case.
When would you recommend buying instead of building?

When the task is common across many companies (meeting notes, generic writing help, simple search over documents) and a tool they already own or can buy does it well enough. We build when the workflow, data or integration is specific to them, or the value depends on how well it fits their systems.

name: UAT, cutover and go-live
title: Implementation: UAT, cutover and go-live
thesis: Going live is a planned sequence, not a button. Users accept the system in UAT, the customer's change board approves a window, the old system is frozen and backed up, data is migrated and reconciled, a named group makes a go or no-go call, traffic switches, and a watched first week follows. At every point there is a way back.
code:
CUTOVER RUNBOOK  Saturday 14 Nov, window 06:00-12:00
06:00  Confirm CAB approval CHG-4471 and on-call names
06:10  Put old system in read-only mode (banner on)
06:15  Take backup; record row counts per table
06:30  Run final delta migration (changes since Friday)
07:30  Reconcile: counts, sums, 50 spot checks
08:00  GO / NO-GO call (sponsor, IT lead, FDE)
08:05  GO: switch feature flag new_claims_ui = on
08:15  Smoke tests: 10 scripted cases pass
08:30  Announce live; hypercare channel open
ROLLBACK trigger: reconcile fails or smoke test fails
ROLLBACK steps: flag off, old system read-write, notify

steps.d: In user acceptance testing (UAT), real users run written test scripts on a test copy with realistic data. They log defects, the team fixes the blocking ones, and the business owner signs that the system is fit to use.

steps.t: The change board approves a window
steps.d: Most enterprises require a change request for production. Their change advisory board (CAB) checks the plan, the risk and the rollback steps, then approves a release window, often a weekend morning.

steps.t: Freeze and back up the old system
steps.d: At the start of the window the old system goes read-only so no new data arrives mid-move. A backup is taken and row counts are recorded, so you have something to compare against and something to restore.
Most data was copied in earlier dry runs. Now only the delta, the records changed since the last copy, is loaded. Because this was rehearsed, you already know it takes about an hour.
Compare the two sides: row counts per table, sums of money columns, and a sample of records checked by hand. Numbers that do not match are a reason to stop, not to hope.
A small named group (sponsor, IT lead, FDE) reviews the criteria agreed in advance: UAT signed, reconciliation passed, rollback tested, on-call named. Each says go or no-go out loud.
If any must-have criterion fails, you roll back: the old system is made read-write again and users carry on as before. A calm no-go is a success of the plan, not a failure of the team.

steps.t: Go: switch traffic and smoke test
steps.d: On go, a feature flag or routing change sends users to the new system. Smoke tests, a short list of scripted checks, confirm the key paths work in production before anyone announces it.
The first week live is watched closely: daily check-ins, a dedicated channel, fast fixes, and sometimes the old process running in parallel. Hypercare ends when agreed exit criteria are met.

ideas: Each environment (dev, test, staging, production) has an owner and a purpose; know who at the customer can grant access and approve changes to each.
Migration is rehearsed: at least one full dry run on a copy, timed, with reconciliation counts, before the real cutover.
UAT is run by the customer's users with written scripts and ends in a signed acceptance, with open defects triaged by severity.
Go or no-go criteria are written and agreed before the day, so the call is a check, not a debate.
Every cutover plan has a tested rollback with a clear trigger and a point of no return.
traps: Treating UAT as a demo: users watch instead of running scripts, so real defects appear in the first week live.
Skipping reconciliation because the migration job said 'success'; a job can succeed and still drop rows.
Having a rollback plan that was never tested, or passing the point of no return without anyone noticing.
qa: What must be true before you say 'go' on cutover day?

The criteria agreed in advance: UAT signed by the business owner with no open blocking defects, migration reconciled (counts, sums, spot checks), rollback tested in staging, a runbook for the day, on-call people named for the first week, and change approval for the window. If a must-have is missing, the answer is no-go or an explicit, signed go with risk.
The migration finishes but the target has 312 fewer rows than the source. What do you do?

Stop before switching traffic. Find which tables differ and whether the missing rows are expected (filtered test data, duplicates removed) or a real loss. If it cannot be explained and fixed inside the window, roll back and reschedule. I never switch users to a system whose data I cannot vouch for.
Why do enterprises have a change advisory board, and how do you work with it?

To control risk in production: they want to know what changes, when, who is affected and how to undo it. I learn their lead time and release windows early, submit a clear change request with the rollback steps and test evidence, and plan the timeline around their calendar instead of fighting it.

name: Support and hypercare
title: Support model, escalation and hypercare
thesis: After go-live, problems reach you as tickets. A clear support model says who answers first (L1), who investigates (L2, often the FDE early on), who changes code (L3 engineering), how severity sets the response time, and how every fix becomes a knowledge-base article so the same ticket never needs an engineer twice.
note: Follow a ticket from the top left. Most tickets should end at L1 (the short vertical path). Only real code defects reach L3, and every fix feeds the knowledge base so L1 can solve it next time. Feature requests leave the ticket flow for the product backlog.
ideas: L1 answers known questions and collects facts, L2 reproduces and fixes configuration or data problems, L3 changes code. In early deployments the FDE often acts as L2.
Severity is about business impact (Sev 1: production down or data wrong for many users; Sev 4: a question), and each level has a response time and an update rhythm.
Fast triage means reproducing the problem with the customer's exact inputs, version and time, before guessing at a cause.
An escalation to your own engineers is a well-written bug report: steps, expected, actual, evidence, impact and what you already tried.
Hypercare is a time-boxed period of extra support after go-live, with written exit criteria and a planned handover to the normal support team.
traps: Letting the customer page the FDE directly for everything, so there is no ticket history and the FDE becomes a single point of failure.
Setting severity by how loud the caller is instead of by impact, which trains everyone to call every issue Sev 1.
Ending hypercare on a date instead of on criteria, so support inherits a system with open issues and no runbook.
qa: What is the difference between response time and resolution time in a support SLA?

Response time is how quickly someone acknowledges the ticket and starts work, for example 30 minutes for Sev 1. Resolution time is how long until it is fixed or a workaround is in place. Most enterprise SLAs promise response times firmly and resolution times only as targets, because some fixes depend on things outside your control.
A customer ticket says 'the assistant gives wrong answers since Tuesday'. How do you triage it?

I ask for two or three specific examples with the exact question, the answer, the time and the user. I check what changed on Tuesday: a release, a prompt change, new documents, an upstream data feed. Then I reproduce one example in a test environment with the same version. Once I can reproduce it, I can set severity by how many users it affects and route it.
How do you know hypercare can end?

When the agreed exit criteria are met: no open Sev 1 or Sev 2 tickets, ticket volume down to a steady level for two weeks, the runbook and knowledge base written and used by the support team, and the support team having solved real tickets without the FDE. Then we do a formal handover meeting.

name: Incidents in the field
title: Incidents and escalations in the field
thesis: When something breaks at a customer, the order matters: declare the incident and name roles, stabilise first (rollback, kill switch, flag), tell the customer early and on a steady timer, work inside their war room and process, fix the cause even if it is theirs, and finish with a blameless review whose actions actually get done.
code:
Subject: [Investigating] Claims assistant errors, Sev 2

What we see: since 09:40 about 30% of summaries fail
Who is affected: claims handlers in the North region
What we are doing: rolled back the 09:30 release;
  checking the document service with your IT team
Workaround: write summaries by hand; no data is lost
Incident lead: Sam Ortiz (ours), Mia Chen (yours)
Next update: 10:45 or sooner if anything changes

steps.d: An alert fires, or a customer user calls to say the tool is failing. Before anyone debugs, someone must decide whether this is an incident: real users are affected now, or soon will be.

Declaring early is cheap. Set a severity, open a channel, and name an incident commander who coordinates, a scribe who keeps the timeline, and a comms lead who talks to the customer. The commander does not debug.

The first goal is to stop the harm, not to understand it. Roll back the last release, turn off a feature flag, or use a kill switch that routes users to the manual process. Diagnosis can wait until users are safe.
Large customers run their own incident process in an IT service management (ITSM) tool with a call or war room. Join it, give your status in their format, and use their ticket number alongside yours.
The first written notice goes out fast, usually within 30 minutes for a high severity: what you see, who is affected, what you are doing, any workaround, and when the next update comes.
Send updates on the promised schedule even when nothing changed. 'No change, still investigating, next update at 11:15' builds more trust than silence. Questions from the bridge feed the next update.

steps.t: Fix the cause, whoever owns it
steps.d: Now diagnose. Sometimes the cause is theirs: an expired certificate, a changed firewall rule, a new data format. Say so with evidence and without blame, and help their team fix it.
When the fix is confirmed, send a resolved notice: start and end time, impact, what fixed it, what users need to do, and when the written review will arrive.

Within a week, review what happened without blaming people: timeline, root cause, contributing factors, and a short list of actions, each with an owner and a date. Then track the actions until they are done.

ideas: Declare an incident as soon as real users are affected; you can always downgrade the severity later.
Separate roles: the incident commander coordinates and decides, others debug, one person owns communication.
Stabilise before you diagnose: rollback, feature flags and kill switches exist so you can stop the harm in minutes.
Customer updates go out on a fixed timer with a promised next update, even when there is no news.
A blameless review looks for how the system allowed the failure, and its actions have owners, dates and follow-up.
traps: Debugging quietly for an hour before telling the customer, who then learns about it from their own users.
The most senior engineer acting as commander and debugger at once, so nobody coordinates or communicates.
Blaming the customer's team in the bridge when the cause is theirs, which turns a shared problem into a fight.
qa: You are on site and the tool you deployed starts returning errors for half the users. What are your first ten minutes?

Confirm it is real and how many users are affected, declare an incident with a severity, and name roles: I take commander unless someone better placed is there. Stabilise first: if a release went out today, roll it back or turn off the flag. Send the customer a first notice with what we see, the workaround, and the time of the next update. Then start diagnosis with the others.
The root cause turns out to be a certificate the customer's IT team let expire. How do you handle it?

State the facts with evidence in the bridge, without blame: the certificate expired at 02:00, here is the error. Offer help renewing it. In the review, treat it as a system gap on both sides: add certificate expiry monitoring on our side and suggest a renewal reminder on theirs. Keeping the relationship matters more than being right.
What makes an incident review 'blameless', and why does it matter?

It asks how the system and process let a normal mistake cause harm, and treats people's actions as reasonable given what they knew. It matters because people then share the real details, which is the only way to find the true causes and fix them.

name: Enablement and the AI CoE
title: Customer enablement and the AI Center of Excellence
thesis: A deployment only pays off if people use it well after you leave. Enablement gives each group (admins, builders, end users) the skills they need, teaches users when to trust the output, builds prompt libraries from their own work, grows internal champions who train others, and sets up a small Center of Excellence that owns intake, standards and learning.
ideas: Enablement is broader than training: it gives people the skills, materials, support and permission to use the tool well, measured by what they can do afterwards.
Admins, builders and end users need different things: operate and govern, extend and fix, use safely in daily work.
The most important user skill is calibrated trust: knowing which outputs to check, how to check them, and when not to use the tool.
Prompt libraries built from the customer's own tasks, with real before-and-after examples, beat generic prompt tips.
A Center of Excellence (CoE) is a small cross-functional group that takes in new ideas, sets standards and spreads what works; champions extend it into every team.
traps: Running one big training session at launch and calling enablement done, so skills fade within weeks.
Teaching features instead of the users' actual tasks, so people pass the session and still cannot do their job with the tool.
Creating a CoE with a charter but no intake process, owner or budget, so it becomes a monthly meeting with no output.
qa: How is enablement different from training?

Training is one activity: teaching a session. Enablement is the whole system that makes people capable: role-specific skills, materials from their own work, champions and office hours for help, and measurement of whether they can actually do the tasks. You judge it by behaviour weeks later, not by attendance.
Users either trust the AI blindly or refuse to use it. What do you teach?

Calibrated trust. I show real examples from their work where the tool is strong and where it fails, teach a quick check for each type of output (for example verify every number against the source), and make it normal to reject a bad answer and report it. I also put confidence cues and sources in the interface so checking is easy.
What does a minimal AI Center of Excellence need to work?

A named lead with some protected time, a few members from IT, security, the business and data, a simple intake form and a monthly review of new ideas using a scoring rubric, a small set of standards (approved tools, data rules, review steps), and a champions network to spread practices. It should publish what it approved and what it learned.
